articles.title: Borneo is burning - living on the frontline of Asia's toxic haze
articles.summary: Months of fires in Indonesia have cloaked Southeast Asia in haze and made hundreds of thousands of people sick.

blocks.text: Firefighters have been battling the stubborn blaze for weeks now
ByLiza TambunanIndonesia correspondent Reporting fromCentral Kalimantan and Gavin Butler

When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.
But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful.

"Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?
"Those thoughts haunt me every night."
Dastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.

Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire nation of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.

But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.

As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five.

"The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week.
"I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dianyra Eka Nastiti is worried about how her children will recover

blocks.text: Dianyra Eka Nastiti is worried about how her children will recover
Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body.

Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.
Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air.

"Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen."
Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.
In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Dastiti says this is unrealistic.

"I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."
Dastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside.
"With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."

Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.

Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.

blocks.caption: Image caption, People have been turning up at hospitals after complaining of feeling sick from the toxic smog

blocks.text: People have been turning up at hospitals after complaining of feeling sick from the toxic smog

Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm.

"If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."
The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.

Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires.

"At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).
"It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."
But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.

For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out – but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat.

"It is truly exhausting," he says, describing how the relentless smoke has produced in him a shortness of breath, a persistent cough and an unshakeable pain in his eyes. When asked what he needs, he says "air".
"The haze makes it hard to breathe," he explains. "We are just hoping for heavy rain."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wildfires have been devastating Indonesia's Central Kalimantan region

blocks.text: Wildfires have been devastating Indonesia's Central Kalimantan region
Thousands of others across Indonesia and Southeast Asia have spent the past several months hoping for the same.

Seasonal wildfires are not new to Indonesia but this year, a so-called Super El Nino has amplified drought conditions and delayed the kind of rainfall that is critical to extinguishing peat fires. It has also made things exponentially harder for those at the coalface, like Juni, who have spent months battling a seemingly irrepressible fire front.
Dr Novita explains that conditions on the ground have become much harsher even in recent weeks, as the prolonged drought makes water increasingly scarce.
Fauzi Rahman, another firefighter in Palangkaraya, highlighted this as one of the main difficulties confronting him and his peers.

"Peatland fires are hard to put out because they require a lot of water and a long time," he says. "On regular land we can clear 20 hectares in a single day, especially with a large team... On peatland, it can take months.
"We really have to inject water deep down, all the way to the bottom, which requires a huge amount of water. And right now, water is hard to find."
What's more concerning for Dr Novita, however, is that her team has reported fires spreading into areas where there has been no history of fire before.
"So we're not only dealing with fires in the usual hotspots but also seeing them emerge in new areas," she says.
In Palangkaraya, people are growing desperate for an end to this apocalypse. But it will likely take a force of nature for that to happen any time soon.

Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office, tells the BBC that "hopefully, with all the extraordinary efforts from the community, the military, and the police working together, the fires can be put out".
"However, as of right now, the fires are still burning," he adds. "So what can we hope for? Our greatest hope is that Almighty God will bring us rain soon."

articles.title: France to deploy troops, admits to failures over weekend unrest
articles.summary: Targeted curfews are implemented to restore calm, with the government admitting to intelligence failures and static police deployments during the unrest

blocks.text: PROTEST. Residents gather during a protest following a fire at the town hall in Limoges, France, October 18, 2026. Reuters
Targeted curfews are implemented to restore calm, with the government admitting to intelligence failures and static police deployments during the unrest

items: France plans to deploy troops alongside police for a massive security operation in response to recent protests and violence in major cities, acknowledging failures in their previous response.

The unrest has been attributed to far-left groups, while the government faces criticism for underestimating public anger over living costs and declining services, leading to heightened tensions ahead of upcoming presidential elections.

Targeted curfews have helped restore calm, but the situation has impacted the economy, with rising borrowing costs and significant losses reported by businesses like Carrefour due to theft and damage.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

PARIS, France – France will reinforce police with troops and mount a huge security operation for more protests planned on Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, October 20, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend’s violence.

“The deployment next Saturday (October 24) will be massive,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities on October 17.

In a sometimes rowdy debate, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the military would be deployed alongside police, while the government pledged to overhaul tactics after widespread criticism that city centers had been left vulnerable.

blocks.caption: France in turmoil: What might follow a weekend of riots?

blocks.text: Framing the crisis as a choice “between violence and the Republic,” Lecornu blamed the unrest on far-left groups, who in turn have accused the government of underestimating public anger over high living costs and declining public services.

The turmoil shocked France because of both its scale and the apparent inability of police to contain it, inflaming tensions ahead of presidential elections next year with candidates from the far right and hard left performing strongly in polls.

Protests in other European countries, including Italy and Albania, have added to concerns that anger over living standards risks spreading around the continent at a time when many nations, including France, are struggling with budget woes.

A night of relative calm in France followed targeted curfews imposed in several areas affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localized curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said.

Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state’s response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not canceling planned police leave.
Nunez apologized for the mistakes. “I deeply regret what happened. I accept my share of responsibility,” he said.

Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence.

Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group.
Sylvain Maillard, a Renaissance deputy for Paris, told Reuters some apps had become “a walkie-talkie system for rioters and looters.”

Underscoring the broad impact of the crisis, French borrowing costs rose further on Tuesday as investors fretted about the prospect of more unrest, with the yield on benchmark 10-year government bonds touching its highest level in 24 years.
Supermarket chain Carrefour said it had lost tens of millions of euros through theft and damage, warning that it faced an “unprecedented situation” because of the disorder.

France’s main student union UNEF has called for further protests on Saturday, pledging to maintain pressure on Macron’s government over what it says is a deteriorating and underfunded education system. “We carry on,” it said on social media.
Separately, groups identifying themselves as “Gilets Jaunes” (Yellow Vests) called for protest actions over rising fuel costs.

The yellow vest movement, largely inactive in recent years, sprang up in 2018 during Macron’s first term over plans to raise petrol taxes. Traffic blockades continued for months until the government made costly concessions it can ill afford now.
Northern Italian cities, including the financial capital Milan, were also hit by riots last weekend.

Though not on the scale seen in France, the unrest nonetheless jolted Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government, which was expected to introduce new security measures at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto described the disturbances as a form of “hybrid warfare” conducted through social media platforms such as TikTok, YouTube and other online networks.

“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras,” Crosetto wrote on X. “The West has yet to realize this or take any meaningful action in response.”

In Milan’s central Corso Vittorio Emanuele II, sportswear retailer On and a Levi’s store that were targeted during the unrest had reopened on Tuesday but remained boarded up. Luxury stores had restored merchandise to window displays after temporarily removing it for security reasons.
In Albania, protesters were expected to take to the streets of Tirana for a seventh consecutive day against the government of Prime Minister Edi Rama. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
articles.summary: The US has advised its citizens to reconsider travelling to Kenya but the government tries to reassure people.

blocks.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images
Nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola
ByBasillioh Rukanga
Reporting fromNairobi
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Should Kenyans be concerned?
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.

With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
What is being done to stop it spreading?
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.

Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.

Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kenya has increased screening at border points

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Kenya has increased screening at border points

In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.

The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Is Kenya prepared in case it starts spreading further?

Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".

The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.

The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Is enough being done to protect health workers?
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.

Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Will there be any restrictions, like a travel ban?
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.

The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kenyan authorities have ruled out travel restrictions

blocks.text: Kenyan authorities have ruled out travel restrictions
Has business and tourism been affected?
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
How many Kenyans are there in DR Congo?
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.

A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.

The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.
How have neighbouring countries responded?
Several countries in the region have announced tightening of surveillance measures and enhanced screening for visitors.
One man who came into contact with the man who died in Kenya is under quarantine in Somalia and samples have been sent to Kenya for testing.

Somalia has also said it was taking precautionary measures, including enhancing surveillance measures at border points "given the evolving regional situation and the movement of people between countries".
The suspected case in Somalia had travelled through Ethiopia, which has also said it had tightened surveillance to prevent an outbreak
In Tanzania, visitors are expected to undergo daily health monitoring for 21 days, through an automated tracking system, which was announced after Kenya confirmed multiple cases of Ebola infections.
Uganda said after Kenya's first Ebola case that it was continuing to "maintain strong surveillance measures to protect public health".
The Kenyan businessman had travelled through Uganda on his way home from DR Congo.
Uganda had reported two Ebola deaths shortly after the outbreak was reported in DR Congo, but the WHO has since declared it to be free of the disease.

Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is located 990 kilometers east of Northern Luzon at 4 am on Wednesday, October 21

items: Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) is expected to bring moderate to heavy rain to at least three provinces in Northern Luzon on Wednesday, October 21.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – At least three provinces in Northern Luzon are expected to have moderate to heavy rain on Wednesday, October 21, as Super Typhoon Rosal (Champi) accelerated before dawn.
As of 4 am on Wednesday, Rosal was already 990 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, moving west northwest at 30 kilometers per hour from the previous 25 km/h.
The super typhoon had intensified further on Tuesday evening, October 20, with its maximum sustained winds reaching 215 km/h from 195 km/h. Its gustiness also went up to 265 km/h from 240 km/h.

Rosal remains unlikely to make landfall in the Philippines, but it will still have an impact due to its size and intensity. It will be closest to extreme Northern Luzon between Thursday, October 22, and Friday afternoon, October 23.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) released an updated rainfall outlook at 5 am on Wednesday, showing that the following provinces are expected to see significant rain:
Wednesday, October 21

items: Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 millimeters): Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

blocks.text: Thursday, October 22

items: Heavy to intense rain (100-200 mm): Batanes
Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Ilocos Norte, Apayao, Cagayan

blocks.text: Friday, October 23

items: Moderate to heavy rain (50-100 mm): Batanes

blocks.text: On Wednesday, aside from the provinces mentioned above, Rosal may trigger moderate to at times heavy rain in Batanes, Isabela, and Catanduanes, as well as scattered rain and thunderstorms in the rest of Cagayan Valley, the rest of Bicol, the rest of the Cordillera Administrative Region, Ilocos Sur, Quezon, and Eastern Visayas.

blocks.text: PAGASA said Rosal can still strengthen further as it moves over the Philippine Sea on Wednesday morning, but it is likely to gradually weaken afterwards. It could weaken into a typhoon on Thursday and into a severe tropical storm by Sunday, October 25.
Rosal’s latest forecast track shows it is projected to maintain its west northwest direction on Wednesday, before heading northwest until Friday morning and recurving northeast by Sunday.
It may leave the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) by Friday evening or early Saturday morning, October 24.

Rosal, which entered PAR on Tuesday, is the Philippines’ 18th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for October. PAGASA earlier estimated the country may have one or two tropical cyclones during the month.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Padayon Cebu: A new space to chat how to make the province more livable
articles.summary: Rappler and civil society groups launch a workspace in the Rappler app to push for a better quality of life in Cebu

blocks.text: Rappler and civil society groups launch a workspace in the Rappler app to push for a better quality of life in Cebu

items: The Padayon Cebu chat room, launched on Rappler's platform, aims to engage Cebuanos in discussions about local issues and solutions, fostering community involvement.
Participants, including civil society groups and experts, are encouraged to share insights and collaborate on addressing challenges like flooding, traffic, and waste management.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

CEBU, Philippines – “Whether making decisions in the community, [or] writing stories that create meaningful impact, all these efforts are more meaningful when the people on the ground are involved and given a platform to speak up,” Luis Calopez, a Cebuano mover said in Rappler’s Padayon Cebu chat room on Friday, October 16.
The young mover is now among more than a hundred Cebuanos who joined the new Padayon Cebu chat room on Muni, a community-building platform found on Rappler’s free app.

In the chat room, attendees of the Move Cebu: Sugbo Alang Sa Sugbuanon forum, Cebu civil society groups, experts, and community leaders have begun conversations on how Cebu can best find solutions to problems its residents face daily — from constant flooding to traffic, to solid waste management.
“It’s really a place where we want facts to thrive,” Rappler’s head of community Pia Ranada said during the launch of the Padayon Cebu chat room at the public forum held on Wednesday, October 14.

blocks.caption: UNITING FOR A BETTER CEBU. The just-launched Padayon Cebu chat room is used as a repository of insights and questions during the Move Cebu public forum on how to improve quality of life in Cebu. Photo by Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler

blocks.text: Ranada explained that amid the ongoing challenges that newsrooms face and the pitfalls of profit-driven algorithms on social media, there needs to be a platform where Cebuanos could freely interact with experts, civil society groups, and journalists to discuss local issues, collaborate on solutions, and keep the province moving forward. (READ: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity)

Padayon Cebu is envisioned to be a “working space” for Cebu citizens who want a place to share their concerns, mobilize for change, and demand for policies and action. Unlike the usual social media platforms, Muni won’t drown out facts and advocacies with micro-targeting and profit-driven feeds.
“For instance, you’re a student who wants to organize a run to make Cebu more walkable, you can share your press release or invite, your sign-up form on the Padayon Cebu chat room,” Ranada said.

Apart from sharing information, the community head emphasized that chat room members could directly ask Rappler’s journalists questions and even offer suggestions on coverage they’re doing in the province.

“It’s a great way for you to stay connected and get verified information about Cebu, and more than that, mobilize your communities to act on problems that you really care about and want to solve,” Ranada said.

Jun Muntuerto, lawyer and convenor of the Cebu Citizens Initiative (CCI), said on the Padayon Cebu chat room on Thursday that the province needs to act now and prepare for harder times due to ongoing international conflicts, trade tensions, and other events affecting the regions.

“Our public life is increasingly drawn toward partisan disputes and preparations for the 2028 elections. Public accountability matters, but Cebu also needs sustained attention to livelihoods, prices, jobs, public services, and emergency readiness,” Muntuerto stressed.

The same sentiments were echoed during Rappler’s huddle with partners and local community leaders on Friday afternoon, October 16. There, the groups identified key issues that affected the province and committed themselves to collaborating and implementing solutions.
“We commit to creative communication campaigns, making space for fisherfolks and also monitoring and evaluation, to constantly document and pursue research studies,” CCI member Kenneth Kabingue said.

“We recommend continuing educational and capacity-building efforts with local communities and working together with government units to tackle the environmental crisis from all facets and entry points where we can,” Vhon Michael Tobes of Zero Hour PH said.
If you’d like to join the conversation on what you can do to help make Cebu more livable, join the Padayon Cebu chat room here. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Elon Musk says Tesla-SpaceX merger being considered
articles.summary: Musk says special committees within both companies have been formed to look at a possible mega-merger.

blocks.text: Elon Musk has said he likes the idea of a merger of Tesla and SpaceX, two of his most notable companies, and it is under active consideration.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said during a call with financial analysts over the quarterly business results of SpaceX on Tuesday.
While Musk noted the certainty of such a merger should not be assumed, and it would need shareholders' support, he said special committees within both companies have been formed to examine the move.

"The special committees have not reached agreement on terms of any transaction and there's no guarantee that they will," Musk added. "But I do think there is a lot of merit to merging and a lot to be gained."
With Tesla valued roughly $1.5 trillion and SpaceX valued at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark one of the largest mergers in history.
Shares of SpaceX rose 8% in after hours trading.
The company, which builds space rockets and Starlink internet satellites, is now expanding into offering cloud compute capacity for other tech companies, like Anthropic and Google.
That line of business has become the most profitable part of SpaceX, bringing in $7.5bn according to the latest quarterly results. Starlink also tallied revenue of $5.2bn.
SpaceX as a whole, however, is not profitable and has lost $1.1bn so far this year.
Shares of Tesla, which reports its own quarterly results on Wednesday, rose 2% after being down slightly for weeks.

Over the last year, Musk has taken to bringing more of his various companies under fewer banners. Before it went public earlier this year, SpaceX acquired xAI and X, the platform formerly known as Twitter, both of which Musk owned.

The recent launch of Terafab, a combined effort to manufacture computer chips between Tesla and SpaceX, was another signal that Musk sees his companies as potentially more effective when working together.
Musk said on Tuesday a full merger between the two companies would make sense for the work each is doing around chips, artificial intelligence, software and more.
Musk, who became the world's first paper trillionaire after the SpaceX stock market debut earlier this year, said he is not included in either of the special committees considering the mega-merger.
He described himself as a "conflicted party" as the chief executive of Tesla and of SpaceX.
Even commenting on the possibility of a merger between the two companies, Musk compared to "tap dancing through a minefield".
He added a merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders. At least 50% of Tesla's shareholders would need to approve the merger, which Musk described as "quite a high hurdle to achieve".
Shareholders have supported Musk's desires before. Last year, a majority of investors in Tesla approved a compensation package for Musk valued around $1 trillion.
While Tesla is known as an electric car company, Musk has lately been shifting resources there to work around robotics.
SpaceX, with its growing focus on AI infrastructure, quickly outstripped Tesla on the stock market in terms of value when it made its stock market debut.

articles.title: Florida kills 77-year-old man in state’s 18th execution of year
articles.summary:
Vietnam veteran William Reaves executed by lethal injection despite letter from fellow veterans urging halt

Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican…

blocks.text: Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican governor Ron DeSantis’s aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.

William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6.12pm following a three-drug injection at Florida state prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River county deputy Richard Raczkowski.
The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6pm execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he said: “No, I do not.”

The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.
A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.

Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over the age of 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s ageing death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.
Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.
Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.

While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.

Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida supreme court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.
The US supreme court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.
The Florida supreme court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.

One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the department of corrections.

The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the US Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves – an army veteran – as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam war. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.

A total of 47 people were executed in the US in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the US so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.
Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on 5 Novemner. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.

articles.title: Is Donald Trump ready to do business with Myanmar?
articles.summary: There are signs the United States is shifting its policy towards Myanmar, formerly a global pariah.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
A top US official recently met with Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing for the first time in years
ByJonathan Head
South East Asia correspondent
Has Washington's long-standing policy of isolating the military regime in Myanmar now changed?
The revelation that a top official in the Trump administration met its leader Min Aung Hlaing last month, and the removal of some business figures from the US sanctions list, suggests that it has.

Until now, the US had had very little official contact with the regime following the 2021 coup, when Myanmar's military ousted democratically-elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi. More recently, it had applied a series of targeted sanctions against those judged to be supporting the junta.

The meeting on 15 and 16 September was with US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance, and it took place in Myanmar's capital Nay Pyi Taw. Its ostensible focus was to secure the release of Adam Castillo, a US citizen who had been detained in June over a dispute with the local American Chamber of Commerce.
But Vance was the most senior US official to meet Min Aung Hlaing since he seized power, and they almost certainly discussed other matters of mutual interest.
Vance is also known to have met Burmese officials in Tokyo in June, again in Tokyo this month, and to have met representatives of the groups opposing military rule.
Signs of a shift in US policy towards Myanmar, though, go back to July last year, at the height of President Donald Trump's tariff war.

That was when Min Aung Hlaing, along with other leaders in the region, received a personal letter from the US president informing him that his country's shattered economy was about to be hit by, in Myanmar's case, 40% tariffs.
Other countries reeled in shock at the punitive levies imposed on their vital trade with a country they had once seen as a friend and ally.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Much of Myanmar has been devastated by a civil war that has been raging since 2021

blocks.text: Much of Myanmar has been devastated by a civil war that has been raging since 2021
But Min Aung Hlaing was delighted.

He replied immediately to express his "sincere appreciation for this encouraging invitation to continue participating in the extraordinary Economy of the United States, the Number One Market in the World", mimicking Trump's hyperbolic phrasing and eccentric capitalisation.
"It is with great esteem that I wish to acknowledge Your Excellency's strong leadership in guiding your country toward national prosperity with the spirit of a true patriot."
This was not just a dictator's hunch that flattery might be the best way to win favours from Trump. Min Aung Hlaing's coup, and the civil war it ignited, had turned him into an international pariah.

His regime was largely unrecognised. He was accused of being a war criminal, with cases lodged against him at the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice. Aside from Russia and, more recently, China, he was shunned by other governments.

Yet here was the US president addressing him just like any other president or prime minister, as "Your Excellency. There was no mention in Trump's letter of the appalling human cost of Min Aung Hlaing's power seizure; of a democracy crushed and leader Aung San Suu Kyi jailed.

That same month the regime signed a $3m (£2.3m) contract with DCI, a long-standing Washington lobbying firm which had been used by a previous Burmese military regime in 2002 to try to improve its image.
Since then the military government has also hired Roger Stone, a controversial lobbyist and confidant of President Trump, at a fee of $50,000 a month.

Also around the same time Adam Castillo, a former US marine and Trump supporter who had just stepped down as president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Yangon, was in Washington trying to persuade Vice President JD Vance's team that it was time to re-engage.
Castillo believed that the US reliance on sanctions to isolate the junta had failed.

"Myanmar mattered to America not only as a morality play but as a strategic interest," he wrote in his book Finding Our Voice: A Story of Leadership in Crisis and the American Spirit Abroad. He discussed with the vice-president's team how the US "could engage Myanmar without war or isolation, loosen China's grip on critical minerals, and align peace with American interests".
Watch: The rebels at the front line of Myanmar's civil war
Castillo was pushing at an open door.

The US dependence on rare earths from China had been exposed when China blocked them in retaliation against Trump's tariffs in April. The administration began prioritising finding alternative sources. Myanmar happens to have large reserves of rare earths which are currently being exploited solely for China's use.

At almost exactly the same time, the state department issued new guidance to US embassies around the world on what to say about elections. From now on, it said, "messages should avoid opining on the fairness or integrity of an electoral process, its legitimacy, or the democratic values of the country in question".

So, when Myanmar held its much-criticised general election in December and January, allowing Min Aung Hlaing to turn himself from coup leader into a notionally civilian president, the US did not, like most Western governments, condemn it as neither free nor fair.
For decades the US has consistently pronounced judgement on other countries' elections. Now the US had nothing to say.
Washington's decision to lift sanctions on some of those targeted by the Biden administration seemed only to confirm the new direction of US-Myanmar policy.

"For years, the US approach to Myanmar has been defined by isolation, sanctions, and distance," wrote the lobbyists DCI in a recent newsletter. "That era is over… thankfully, President Trump has the courage to try something different."
The tone is certainly different, but not so much the substance of US-Myanmar relations.

"In practice less has changed than the headlines suggest," says Richard Horsey, Myanmar adviser for the International Crisis Group, adding that Min Aung Hlaing is still sanctioned. "What is new is the level of contact and the location. Senior US officials have now been to Nay Pyi Taw, which is exactly what Min Aung Hlaing wanted. What he wants next is sanctions relief, and that will be harder."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Myanmar's leader Min Aung Hlaing on a recent diplomatic visit to Malaysia

blocks.text: Myanmar's leader Min Aung Hlaing on a recent diplomatic visit to Malaysia

It was another Trump initiative last year, though, which has arguably had a much greater impact on Myanmar: the dismantling of USAID, which slashed aid to opposition groups, dissident media and refugees by more than half.

There was also the decision, decried by human rights groups, to withdraw Temporary Protected Status from 4,000 Burmese who had sought sanctuary in the US. This has left them living in fear of being sent back, where many face being jailed, or worse.
As for the rare earths in Myanmar, few experts believe they will ever be of much use to the US. Most lie in areas contested by ethnic insurgent armies.

They are currently extracted by Chinese companies with long experience of operating in these lawless borderlands, and transported over the border to China for processing. It is difficult to see how the US could get access to them.
It is also doubtful that the US will get meaningful co-operation from the Myanmar government in combating the scam industry.

There have been a few highly-publicised actions against some of the larger scam compounds, but the syndicates running them have simply dispersed to smaller operations in more remote areas, and in any case most are run with the support of militia groups allied to the Myanmar military.
"Talking to Nay Pyi Taw is not wrong in itself," says Hunter Marston, Southeast Asia director at the Lowy Institute.

"The question is what Washington asks for and what it gives away. It should use the channel for the things that matter most: humanitarian access, an end to airstrikes on civilians. It should keep talking to the opposition and the ethnic armed groups, who hold much of the country. And on scams, the most effective thing the US can do is to co-ordinate with other governments in the region, including China, to go after the money."

Perhaps the bigger question, though, is whether President Trump, distracted by domestic politics and the war on Iran, has the capacity to give any sustained attention to Myanmar, let alone enough to challenge the dominant influence of China.

articles.title: Odds of fifth interest rate hike this year likely to shorten as RBA deputy warns inflation outlook ‘worsening’
articles.summary:
Andrew Hauser says the central bank faces ‘hard choices’ as it looks to balance the risks of entrenched inflation with the desire to protect the labour market

Andrew Hauser, the Reserve…

blocks.text: Andrew Hauser, the Reserve Bank’s deputy governor, has reignited talk of a fifth interest rate hike on Melbourne Cup day, warning of “hard choices” ahead in response to an inflation outlook that “looks materially worse” than the central bank had expected two months ago.

Hauser, speaking at an investment bank conference in Sydney on Wednesday morning, said the RBA monetary policy board members were juggling a slowing economy with fears that Australians were starting to lose faith in the central bank’s ability to bring inflation back to the 2.5% target.
The deputy governor sits on the RBA’s monetary policy board, which begins its next two-day meeting on 2 November.
Financial markets earlier on Wednesday morning were pricing in a nearly one-in-three chance of a hike to 4.85% but those odds are likely to shorten after Hauser’s comments.

“The basic fact [is] that inflation has been high for a very long time now, and we are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we’re going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period,” he said.
Businesses were starting to see 3.5% inflation as the “new normal”, Hauser said. Removing an entrenched inflation psychology could require higher interest rates, he warned.
Hauser said while inflation was clearly too high, the picture for the economy was “more mixed”.
“Clearly, we need a period of below-trend growth to bring inflation down, and we’re seeing that happening,” he said.

High interest rates and high petrol prices were weighing on activity, Hauser said. Last week’s jobs figures – which showed unemployment reaching a five-year high of 4.7% – were “a little bit weaker than people had expected”.

But Hauser pointed to surprisingly strong economic growth among Australia’s major trading partners in Asia, and the boom in datacentre investment. Oil prices were about a third higher than the bank had predicted in August.
This created the difficult trade-offs facing the RBA’s rate-setting board, he said. “Do you do more to tackle higher inflation, recognising that that means weaker activity, a weaker labour market?

“Or do we hold our horses to protect the labour market … mindful of the potential that there may be more downside momentum of the economy, but accept the risks in so doing that this upside inflation risk embeds [into Australians’ expectations], and that becomes more expensive to deal with?”
He added: “Those are hard choices. They’re not where we’d like to be ideally as the central bank, but I think that’s the that’s what we’re facing into as we as we meet the week after next.”

articles.title: Alabama governor commutes sentence of prisoner on death row
articles.summary:
Toforest Johnson’s death penalty reduced to life in prison without parole over doubts about his conviction

Toforest Johnson, an Alabama death row inmate, will no longer face execution after…

blocks.text: Toforest Johnson, an Alabama death row inmate, will no longer face execution after the state’s Republican governor commuted his sentence amid increasing doubts about his conviction.

Kay Ivey, the Alabama governor, commuted Johnson’s sentence to life in prison without parole in the 1995 murder of William Hardy, a Jefferson county deputy sheriff. Johnson has long maintained he is innocent, and several former public officials, as well the local district attorney, have argued he should receive a new trial.

“When presented with Mr Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment – death,” Ivey said in a statement. “My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole.”

Ivey has overseen 27 executions during her time as governor, and commuted the death sentence of three death row inmates. Her decision on Tuesday comes shortly after another Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, cancelled a planned execution for the first time earlier this month.

Ty Alper, one of Johnson’s attorneys, said they are grateful to Ivey for “diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution”. Alper said the fight to overturn the conviction will continue. The governor only has the power to commute a death sentence in such cases.
“Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” Alper said.
Johnson was sentenced to death in 1998.

Hardy was shot twice in the head while working off-duty security at a hotel in 1995. Johnson has maintained he was on the other side of town at the time of the shooting. No physical evidence tied him to the killing, and more than 10 witnesses placed him on the other side of town during the killing.

Danny Carr, the Jefferson county district attorney, has called for the conviction to be overturned, as has the original prosecutor. Carr has said that “the foundation of this conviction has disintegrated” and that there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness.

The witness at Johnson’s 1998 trial testified that, while eavesdropping on a phone call, she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the crime. She was paid $5,000 in 2001 for her testimony, and Johnson’s lawyers argue that the state withheld evidence of monetary motivation for the testimony.

There has been a years-long legal effort to win a new trial in the case that has garnered national attention, including support from Kim Kardashian, and was the subject of a podcast. Carr wrote in a 2024 court filing that the “evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years”.

Former judges and prosecutors have joined the effort seeking a new trial for Johnson. Bill Baxley, a former Alabama attorney general, former state chief justices Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers, and several former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials supporting a new trial.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Pamela Wallin says it was simply 'time to move on' after surprise resignation from Senate
articles.summary: Wallin was appointed Consul General of Canada to New York after 9/11 by former Prime Minister Chrétien. She became one of Canada's best-known broadcast journalists during her time hosting CTV's…

image.caption: Pamela Wallin advocated for an expansion to Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) during her time in the Senate. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New

Wallin was appointed Consul General of Canada to New York after 9/11 by former Prime Minister Chrétien. She became one of Canada's best-known broadcast journalists during her time hosting CTV's Canada AM and as that network's Ottawa bureau chief.
Former broadcast journalist says she's not sure what she'll do next
Pamela Wallin says it was just time to resign.
After 17 years sitting as a Saskatchewan senator in the chamber of sober second thought, she wanted to move on to other opportunities.
She said that, contrary to public perception, a senator’s duties are “24-7” and she needed time to figure out what comes next.
“You know when a job has come to an end and it’s time to move on in your own head and that’s just where I was,” Wallin, 73, told Blue Sky’s Leisha Grebinski.
“I have other things to do that I want to try.”
Pamela Wallin on why she left the Senate and what's next for Canada
Wide-ranging career
Wallin has spent her adult life in the public eye.

Born in Moose Jaw, she was raised in Wadena, 222 kilometres northeast of Regina, before moving to Ontario where she spent 40 years in broadcast journalism, including hosting CTV’s Canada AM, working as that network’s first female bureau chief in Ottawa and co-anchoring CBC’s nightly national newscast Prime Time News.
She served as Consul General of Canada to New York after 9/11, appointed to the position by then-prime minister Jean Chrétien.

Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper appointed her to the Senate in 2008. Unlike her high-profile career in journalism, her time as a senator has been quieter, according to Greg Poelzer, a political scientist and professor at the University of Saskatchewan.

“I think she was one of the more quiet senators and not really known for making a big impact, say on advancing or supporting new legislation that came into law,” Poelzer told CBC’s Peter Mills on The 306.
Wallin’s time in the Senate was marred by her involvement in the 2013 Senate expense scandal.

items: Senate rejects calls for outside oversight of expenses

blocks.text: An audit determined Wallin improperly charged to the Senate about $140,000 in travel expenses related to her work on corporate boards.
Wallin repaid the money, plus interest, and said she had made a mistake in filing the paperwork.
LISTEN | Greg Poelzer and host Peter Mills discuss Wallin's resignation on The 306:
The 3069:28Pamela Wallin resigns from Senate
Advocacy
Poelzer said Wallin was a vocal advocate in recent years for expanding access to Canada’s Medical Assistance In Dying (MAID) program.

Wallin’s mother had Alzheimer’s, and the former journalist wanted the program to expand and allow people in the early stages of the disease, and others like it, to be able to pre-authorize their medically assisted death.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced earlier this month that Ottawa will introduce legislation that would “open the door” for advance consent for MAID in situations where their disease will eventually impair a person's capacity for consent.

items: Premier who oversaw Canada's first assisted dying law says he worries it's gone too far
Government to reveal next steps for medically assisted dying, justice minister says

blocks.text: Wallin said the proposed expansion of MAID, something she’d spent 11 years fighting for, seemed like a good time to wrap up her time in the Senate.
“I’d given my final speech on that topic on the Wednesday evening," Wallin said. "Some little tiny part of my brain said ‘take the win and move on.’”
Wallin’s resignation caught many, including Poelzer, by surprise. She still had nearly two years left before hitting the Senate’s mandatory retirement age of 75.
“Normally you would expect a person to complete the term,” Poelzer said.
“That’s the part that caught a lot of people by surprise, because she’s about 18 months, two years away from her term completing.”
Saskatchewan now has two vacant Senate seats: Wallin’s and the seat belonging to Todd Lewis, who died in July.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Colleen Silverthorn is a journalist for CBC in Regina. Colleen comes from the newspaper world, where she primarily covered politics and business. She has worked in Saskatoon, Regina and London, England. Story ideas? Email colleen.silverthorn@cbc.ca
with files from Peter Zimonjic, Blue Sky and the 306

articles.title: Portugal housing protests continue after police clear camps
articles.summary: Demonstrators vow to continue their campaign to call for affordable housing in Portugal after police cleared tent camps and arrested at least 55 people.

image.caption: Protesters take to the streets in Lisbon to demand affordable housingImage: Patricia De Melo Moreira/AFP

blocks.text: Thousands of people rallied in Lisbon, Porto and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled protest camps and arrested a total of 55 demonstrators.
The protesters vowed to continue their campaign against Portugal's deepening housing crisis, which has made buying or renting a home increasingly unaffordable.
Organizers said more than 1,000 people gathered in each of the two main protest locations, although police did not provide crowd estimates.

blocks.caption: Protesters call for affordable housing as soaring property prices put pressure on residents Image: Pedro Nunes/REUTERS

blocks.text: In Lisbon's central Rossio square, demonstrators voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp on Wednesday.
Police moves to shut down protest camps
Police launched coordinated operations in Lisbon and Porto shortly before 6 a.m. (0500 GMT) on Tuesday, after warning protesters that their camps were illegal.
Activists had occupied Lisbon's Rossio square since Saturday, setting up around 200 tents. In Porto, protesters had camped in Dom Joao I square for about 10 days.

blocks.caption: Protesters set up tents in Lisbon's Rossio square before police moved to eject people from the central square on Tuesday [FILE: October 19, 2026]Image: Patricia De Melo Moreira/AFP

blocks.text: Authorities seized 228 camping structures during the operation.
In Porto, demonstrators dismantled their tents themselves after police threatened to intervene. In Lisbon, officers cleared the square as protesters formed a human chain.
Clashes subsequently broke out, according to footage broadcast by local television stations.
Carla Valadao, a spokesperson for the Lisbon camp, described the operation as "very aggressive."
However, Public Security Police superintendent Sergio Soares disputed that account, saying the eviction had been "calm, proportionate and appropriate, with no police charge."
All 55 people arrested were later released pending a court appearance in Lisbon on Wednesday.
Why are people protesting in Portugal?
Portugal is struggling with one of Europe's worst housing affordability crises.
Property purchase prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new leases have nearly doubled over the same period.
The problem is particularly severe in major cities such as Lisbon and Porto, where residents have also protested against excessive tourism and an influx of so-called digital nomads.

blocks.caption: Protesters camp out in Porto [PHOTO: October 19]Image: Diogo Baptista/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Demonstrators accuse the center-right government of failing to address the crisis.
They are demanding the withdrawal of a bill that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The proposed legislation has already passed its first parliamentary reading.
Debora Miranda, a 41-year-old communications consultant, told Reuters she joined the Lisbon demonstration to represent generations struggling with rising housing costs.
"If people don't feel at home, in every sense of the word, they can't move forward with their lives...enough is enough."
Jorge Paixao, a 19-year-old history student, described the situation as "a societal crisis."
He said his generation needed "the ability to live with dignity, start families and rejuvenate Portugal."
Portugal housing protest takes place amid demos around Europe
The demonstrations come amid growing anger over housing affordability and living costs across several European countries.
Protesters in Portugal have sought to align their movement with similar demonstrations in neighboring Spain.
In Madrid, activists maintain a tent camp to call for stronger action to tackle the housing crisis. The crisis was sparked by the eviction ofMaria del Carmen Abascal from her home.

blocks.caption: Protesters call for stronger laws to protect renters [PHOTO: October 16, Madrid]Image: Bernat Armangue/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The nearly four weeks of protests in Spain have contributed to political turmoil, leading to a snap general election being called for November 29.
Meanwhile, demonstrations over rising living costs have also taken place in France, Belgium and Italy.

Violence that erupted in France over the weekend on the sidelines of otherwise peaceful protests has raised concerns that similar unrest could spread to other countries facing comparable economic pressures.

articles.title: ADL condemns Trump’s antisemitic slur but fails to mention him by name
articles.summary:
Anti-Defamation League post decries ‘shylock’ slur but does not explain that president used it at Kansas rally on Monday

The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) denounced the use of the term…

blocks.text: The Anti-Defamation League (ADL) denounced the use of the term “shylock” as antisemitic on Tuesday, without explaining that the slur had been used a day earlier by Donald Trump in a speech in Kansas.

Trump used the slur during a Monday night rally in support of Republican senator Roger Marshall, who is locked in a closer-than-expected re-election fight against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. Marshall, a doctor, as been criticized for filing lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills, leading to 18 of them being arrested.
Trump said Marshall’s critics, by highlighting the patient lawsuits in campaign ads, “made it like, oh, he was some kind of a shylock-type guy”.
Trump also falsely claimed Marshall was “mandated by law” to “go after those people”.

The ADL’s brief social media post made no mention of Trump at all. The organization, founded to combat antisemitism, offered no explanation as to why it found it necessary to explain that anyone equating an avaricious person to Shylock, the villainous Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice, is using an antisemitic trope.

“The term ‘Shylock’ is rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype,” the ADL posted on X but not its other social media accounts. “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community.”

Critics who accuse the ADL of using accusations of antisemitism selectively, to attack people who are critical of Israel, suggested that the Jewish American civil rights group was going easy on Trump because of his support for Israel.
Trump’s use of the slur came just a day after he had endorsed Israel prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the country’s elections.

Matt Duss, a former foreign police adviser to senator Bernie Sanders, the most prominent Jewish American politician, responded to the ADL’s failure to mention Trump by suggesting its president would have been more direct had someone else used the slur.

“If a Democrat said it, [ADL CEO] Jonathan Greenblatt would be knocking people over to get in front of a camera to condemn them by name, but it was Trump, so it’s just a general public service announcement,” Duss wrote.

In 2014, after then vice-president Joe Biden described people who take financial advantage of American service members as “shylocks”, the Anti-Defamation League’s national director accepted his apology and called the remarks “a teachable moment”.

Trump previously used the slur during a 2025 rally in Iowa. The US president told supporters that eliminating the taxes on inherited family farms would save farmers from “going to the banks and borrowing from, in some cases a fine banker, and in some cases shylocks and bad people”.

The day after that Iowa rally, the ADL called the president’s use of the term “very troubling and irresponsible”, but Trump claimed ignorance when he was asked by a reporter if he had intended to use the word “shylocks” to refer to Jews.

“No, I’ve never heard it that way,” Trump replied then. “To me, a shylock is somebody that’s a, uh, a moneylender at high rates. I’ve never heard it that way. You view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.”

articles.title: ‘I forgot to pay’: Victoria’s premier Ben Carroll drives off without paying for petrol, sparking police inquiries
articles.summary:
After being contacted by officers, politician says, he has paid bill and is ‘grateful for the team at the servo for their understanding’

  • Get our

blocks.text: On Tuesday night, Ben Carroll received a phone call: police were looking for him.
The Victorian premier had met with the state’s police commissioner earlier that morning – so he wasn’t exactly hard to find.

But the officers weren’t looking to speak to him about their resources, powers or investigations. They wanted to know if he had driven off from a service station without paying for his petrol on Monday night.
“Late Monday night, I was running some errands and filled up the car with petrol,” Carroll said in a statement early on Wednesday morning.
“[I] found out yesterday I forgot to pay. I fixed the bill straight away.”
He added that he was “grateful for the team at the servo for their understanding”.

It’s understood Carroll had filled up his car near his home in his electorate of Niddrie on Monday night, after spending the evening responding to the alleged attack on the federal MP Helen Haines in regional Victoria earlier that day.

Unbeknown to him – as he met with Victoria police commissioner, Mike Bush, the head of the Australian federal police, Krissy Barrett, and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese – officers had begun searching for him.
It’s understood they contacted him through the Department of Parliamentary Services on Tuesday night.
A bashful Carroll then headed back to the service station to pay up.
No further action is expected to be taken.
after newsletter promotion

Speaking at an event on Wednesday, Carroll said the former deputy premier John Thwaites had contacted him to say: “Don’t worry, Ben. I didn’t pay for the petrol, and I also drove off with the nozzle in the car.”
“That made me feel a lot better,” Carrol told the Age forum. “It shows that politicians are human beings, and even premiers make mistakes.”
Asked about the matter on Wednesday, Bush said the view of police was that a petrol drive-off was a “civil matter unless it’s proven otherwise”.
“If someone does something accidentally, non-deliberately, it becomes a very civil matter,” the commissioner said. “That civil redress is available, and I do understand that civil redress was made.

“It does occur and that’s why we’re very careful not to criminalise every petrol driver. We do understand, and I’m very empathic and sympathetic to petrol station owners who do suffer, but it’s not always criminal [behaviour].”
It came months after Carroll’s predecessor, Jacinta Allan, told parliament that police were grappling with a rise in illegal drive-offs from petrol stations.
“We are seeing a rise in incidents of drive-offs at service stations, and it is an illegal practice,” she said in March.

articles.title: Australian researchers identify new subtype of depression linked to body clock disruptions
articles.summary:
Study identifies ‘circadian depression’ as affecting nearly a quarter of more than 11,000 participants

  • Get our
articles.byline: Donna Lu assistant editor, climate, environment and science

blocks.text: Australian researchers have identified a new subtype of depression – termed “circadian depression” – linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock, which they believe is less responsive to traditional antidepressant treatments.

In a study published in British Journal of Psychiatry, involving clinical and genetic data from 11,380 Australians with mostly severe and recurrent depression, researchers identified circadian depression as affecting nearly a quarter (23%) of participants.
They suggest people affected by the subtype may benefit from treatments that target the body’s circadian rhythms, such as melatonin and light therapy.

While a link between mood disorders and disrupted daily rhythms has been known for some time, the researchers say the “study strengthens the evidence base for a circadian subtype of depression as a biologically valid and clinically useful phenotype of depression”.

The study’s first author, Dr Emiliana Tonini of the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre, said the researchers defined circadian depression as being in participants who showed at least three out of six features: experiencing a seasonal pattern of illness, delayed sleep timing, sleeping longer when depressed, being a night owl, waking feeling very tired, and social jetlag – when “their sleep when they go to bed during the week or when they work is very different from the weekend or when they are free to organise their day”.

“Individuals with circadian depression have more severe mental health symptoms,” Tonini said during a press briefing. “The age of onset of their depression was younger compared to those with non-circadian depression, but they also had more episodes and also more complex trajectories, more suicidality, more hypomanic and psychotic-like symptoms as well.”

The researchers also found that those with circadian depression had higher genetic risk for ADHD and mood disorders, “but also a series of metabolic and inflammatory markers”, Tonini said. “This is important because that indicates that circadian depression is not just depression with bad sleep, but actually there is an underlying biology that is quite distinct from other forms of depression.”

The researchers hope that being able to clinically diagnose circadian depression in future may help with more tailored treatments, particularly for young people seeking mental health support for the first time.

Prof Ian Hickie, a psychiatrist and co-director of the Brain and Mind Centre, said: “What is critical about being in this circadian type is its poor response to the standard therapies, those which are typically recommended in the guidelines.”
SSRIs and SNRIs, typical first-line antidepressant drugs, were less effective and had more side effects for people with the circadian subtype, the study found.

For those with circadian depression, “chronobiological treatments – things focused on the sleep-wake cycle, particularly … to do with morning light exposure, daylight activity, regularity of sleep-wake cycles, regularity of food schedules, is critical”, Hickie said.

In their study, the researchers noted that the participants were “were limited to those of genetically inferred European ancestry, which may limit generalisability”, and that “future studies are needed to replicate our findings in diverse samples”.
The director of the Monash Alfred Psychiatry Research Centre, Prof Jayashri Kulkarni, who was not involved in the research, described it as a “really well-conducted study”.

“They have got a polygenic risk score, which means that they’ve actually managed to tie certain types of depression to a specific genetic profile,” she said. “That will be important for onward treatment.”

The research did not take into account the hormonal impacts of menopause, Kulkarni added, “which is predominantly one of the things that women describe as causing sleep disturbance … That would be another factor that might be worth considering.”

Prof Andrew Coogan, a behavioural neuroscientist at Maynooth University in Ireland, said: “We have known for a long time that major depression is linked to changes in the body clock that make people later to bed and later to rise so the findings are not overly surprising.”
He cited a “lack of detail as to how the cluster of features of, and the criteria for, the proposed circadian subtype of depression was arrived at”.
“The results of this exploratory study are best interpreted as initial if interesting findings that warrant further examination,” he said.
