articles.title: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy
articles.summary:
Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’

The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv…

blocks.text: The US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.

He said Ukraine was again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, saying the US move would save lives.
The Ukrainian president added: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”

The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needed a new leader.

The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.

Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”

He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.

Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.

Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, the Wall Street Journal reported.
“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”

The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.

Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.

The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.

“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.
Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.
US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.

Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.

At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.

articles.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
articles.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.
The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.
The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
The White House has been contacted for comment.

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.
Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.
"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.
The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".
The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.
Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.
"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.
The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.
"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.
The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

articles.title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau
articles.summary:
Police seized dozens of hepatitis B vaccines from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns

Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy…

blocks.text: Controversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officials said on Facebook.

The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.

The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.

The Bandim Health Project recently posted a letter of approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, also approved the study earlier this month.
Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government, disputed reports that the trial would move forward.
“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.

The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.

Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.

Through its country office in Guinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.
The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.

Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, calling them “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several times referenced the results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’s podcast in 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.

Stabell Benn was a member of the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) who said she wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.

The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to a report from the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is now fundraising to help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.

“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”

The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.

“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.

articles.title: Nigeria records its first Ebola case, in capital Abuja
articles.summary: Nigeria has reported its first known case of Ebola during Africa's latest outbreak originating in the DRC. Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said the patient was a woman who had recently flown to…

image.caption: The vast majority of the known Ebola cases in the outbreak are still located in the Democratic Republic of Congo, but the number of affected countries is rising [FILE: October 19, 2026]Image: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nigeria's Health Ministry on Tuesday confirmed that the country had recorded its first known case of Ebola in the current outbreak. A woman who recently arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.

The outbreak is thought to have started in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, not far from the Ugandan border, with Uganda the second country to record infections. It also recently spread to Kenya in limited numbers, with nine known cases recorded this month.
The overwhelming majority of known cases, however, remain confined to the DRC, particularly its eastern provinces.
Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak
What do we know about the Nigerian case of Ebola?
Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate said that the patient was a woman who had "recently arrived on an international flight from Uganda."

She first began to exhibit symptoms on October 7, and was admitted to a private Abuja hospital on October 11, before being tested and diagnosed with Ebola. He said authorities had already begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient.
"We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all contacts the individual may have had," he said.

Nigeria's Center for Disease Control said two weeks ago that it was stepping up surveillance after the first recorded cases in Kenya, saying it was improving the country's preparedness for a possible outbreak.

"These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of healthcare workers," the agency said.
Nigeria created an Ebola task force in June.

"We do not want a repeat of what happened during the last outbreak when a carrier entered the country, and everyone was scrambling to respond," Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to President Bola Tinubu, said when the task force was announced. "We have covered a lot of ground and established structures to address any potential threat."

blocks.caption: Kenya has also been put on alert this month after identifying a cluster of nine cases, which officials believe all revolve around one initial patientImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Over 9,000 cases in current outbreak, the fastest-growing on record
While Ebola does not spread as readily as highly contagious viruses like the flu or COVID, it is considerably more dangerous to those who do contract it.
The current outbreak, involving a lesser-known strain, the Bundibugyo Ebolavirus, has led to more than 9,000 confirmed cases and more than 4,300 deaths, a fatality rate of almost 50%.

Almost all the cases and deaths are confined to the DRC, even as more countries become involved. The first patient in Kenya died, and authorities believe the other eight known cases are all part of a cluster beginning with him. They say there's no sign of a spread beyond his contacts.

Uganda, which borders the Ituri province outbreak epicenter in DRC, reported 20 cases and two deaths quite much earlier this year. It was then declared Ebola-free in late August by the World Health Organization after reaching 42 days since a confirmed case. Tuesday's case in Nigeria could potentially put this status back into question, given the Health Ministry's comments on the patient's travel history.
This year's outbreak is already the second-largest on record and by far the fastest-spreading — although modestly improved testing and diagnostic capacity may also contribute to the higher numbers.

The West African Ebola epidemic of 2014-16 led to around 11,300 deaths from around 28,500 cases — but that was over a span of around 30 months. This outbreak was first declared in May of this year, although researchers believe it likely began in small numbers of cases several months earlier.
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?

articles.title: Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with MS
articles.summary: After five years of tireless advocacy for those who shared her diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Christina Applegate has revealed that doctors now believe she was misdiagnosed.

image.caption: Christina Applegate, seen here in January 2020, says her doctors have found that she was misdiagnosed when told she had multiple sclerosis in 2021. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
After five years of tireless advocacy for those who shared her diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, Christina Applegate has revealed that doctors now believe she was misdiagnosed.
Initially diagnosed in 2021, actress says she now has no answer for ongoing symptoms
After five years of tireless advocacy for those who shared her diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS), Christina Applegate has revealed that doctors now believe she was misdiagnosed.
“To me it comes as, like, I’m back at square one,” she said of the news.

Applegate shared the story in a two-part Tuesday episode of the podcast MeSsy, which she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who has MS. She had spent some months away from the show, which she explained was partially to process the revelation.
Audibly emotional at times, Applegate said that while her doctor had congratulated her when revealing she didn’t have MS, she didn't feel happy — only lost.
“You don’t get misdiagnosed and all of a sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … if anything, I’ve gotten worse, in some ways,” she said.
“My legs aren’t working, you know, all the same stuff is happening to me.”

Multiple sclerosis is a complex autoimmune disease of the central nervous system. With MS, the immune system mistakenly attacks the myelin, part of the central nervous system that serves as a protective coating for the nerves. This inhibits the brain and the body from sharing information, resulting in symptoms including numbness, pain, memory issues, fatigue and mobility issues.
The disease takes many forms, with some patients experiencing periods of remission and relapse, and others dealing with more consistent progression causing increasing disability.

Misdiagnosis is not uncommon globally — one study from 2019 by researchers at Cedars-Sinai found that the rate of misdiagnosis was nearly one in five patients. A 2024 review looked at studies reporting misdiagnosis rates ranging from five to 41 per cent, and found an estimate of 15 per cent misdiagnosis rate when they pooled six studies.
Applegate arrives for the 29th Screen Actors Guild Awards in Century City, Calif., in February 2023. (Valerine Macon/AFP via Getty Images)
'It's been a tough road'
Applegate first announced she had MS on social media in August 2021, saying at the time that “it’s been a tough road.”
In Tuesday’s podcast episode, she said that it all started in January 2021, when she began to experience numbness in her feet, which slowly moved up her legs.
“And then the pain started,” she said. “All that time, I was being tested for everything under the sun.”

items: Man who lost legs to MS warming heads and hearts by knitting tuques on custom-made cot
Mom's multiple sclerosis journey an inspiration for Vancouver Goldeneyes goalie
The subject of Lyme disease is littered with misinformation. Celebrities are part of the problem, experts say

blocks.text: She said she underwent spinal MRIs, brain MRIs and a spinal tap, and that doctors thought she might have a low-grade version of the disease at first. But her symptoms kept getting progressively worse. When doctors found nearly 40 lesions on her brain, she was officially diagnosed with MS.
“I felt like, 'OK, I have an answer,'” she said in the podcast episode.

But a few years in, her doctor paused her infusion treatments to see how her B cells would respond. When their levels didn’t change, doctors began to look closer at the diagnosis. Ultimately, it was concluded she didn’t have MS — but she wasn’t given another diagnosis to replace it, leaving her in the dark as to what was causing her ongoing symptoms.
Applegate attends the 26th Annual Screen Actors Guild Awards in Los Angeles in January 2020. (Mike Coppola/Getty Images for Turner)

“I feel like I let everybody down, you know?” Applegate said tearfully to co-host Sigler, saying she felt like they’d become “the poster children for MS” together. The two started their podcast in 2024, featuring conversations about parenting and ordinary life struggles while dealing with the disease.
“It’s like I had a reason … for why my day sucked every day, and now I don’t have a reason. It’s very unnerving and it’s really confusing for me.”

The actress, who announced she was stepping away from the screen in 2021 with her diagnosis, is known for roles in movies such as Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy, and Bad Moms, and for TV roles including her Emmy-nominated turn in Netflix’s Dead to Me.
Global rates of MS

Globally, more than 3.1 million people are living with MS worldwide, according to MS International Federation. Canada has one of the highest rates of the disease in the world, with more than 90,000 Canadians, roughly one in 400, affected by it. Around seven out of 10 cases are among women.

“I’m going to continue holding in my heart that this is a blessing for you,” Sigler said.

articles.title: No Canada-U.S. trade deal expected before American midterm elections: sources
articles.summary: The Canada-U.S. trade war is poised to grind on for the foreseeable future, as sources tell CBC News hope of a deal before the American midterm elections has completely faded.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump is seen with U.S. Sen Eric Schmitt as he arrives in Kansas for a campaign rally on Thursday. Sources tell CBC News that the White House is fully focused on the midterms, which are now two weeks away. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

blocks.text: The Canada-U.S. trade war is poised to grind on for the foreseeable future, as sources tell CBC News hope of a deal before the American midterm elections has completely faded.

According to three sources with knowledge of the situation, Canadian government officials have been informing industry groups over the past few weeks that there is no expectation a deal can be reached before the Nov. 3 vote.
There is no substantial engagement at this time, according to the sources, even though officials from both countries remain in contact.

The sources have also been told that the White House is fully immersed in the election campaign. U.S. President Donald Trump is spending much of his time on the road holding rallies, as polls suggest his Republican Party is facing an uphill battle to maintain control of the House and possibly even the Senate.

items: Michigan Republican Senate candidate breaks with Trump on trade war
Trump's tariffs are unpopular in Maine. A Republican senator may pay the price

blocks.text: CBC News agreed not to name the sources as they were not authorized to speak publicly about this active and sensitive issue.

"There was some optimism within some parts of the [federal] government and in certain parts of Canadian industry that we might have seen a deal ahead of the midterms," said Brian Clow, who was former prime minister Justin Trudeau's deputy chief of staff.
"But that window appears to be entirely closed."

The optimism was rooted in the idea that because the trade war with Canada is unpopular with some American voters — those who blame Trump's trade and tariff policies for an increase in the cost of living — the Trump administration would be motivated to cut a deal.
Inflation top of mind for voters ahead of U.S. midterms

The trade war with Canada is unpopular enough that some Republican candidates have distanced themselves from the president and his agenda. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine is among the Republicans who have publicly pushed back as she finds herself in a tight re-election race.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc confirmed that the government isn't expecting a deal before the midterm elections in an interview with CBC's Power & Politics following publication of this story.

"We have continued to remain engaged with the United States. But we're not going to rush into some particular circumstance and … agree to something that we don't think is in Canada's sovereign interest or economic interest," he told host David Cochrane.
Trump will keep Trumping, regardless of result
Whatever the results of the midterm elections may be, Clow said that Canadians should not anticipate much change when it comes to trade.
He suggests the Democrats taking power away from Republicans would provide "a marginal benefit to Canada" at best.

He says Trump could be distracted if a Democrat-led House or Senate launches investigations into his administration. They also could pass legislation that attempts to rein in some of Trump's policies.
However, Trump has already signalled he will veto anything he doesn't like.

"He still has a lot of tools to inflict a lot of damage on Canada and the rest of the world when it comes to trade," Clow said. "I expect no matter what happens … he's still going to use those tools."

Trump has carried out his tariff strategy using executive orders, along with actions by the U.S. Commerce Department and the U.S. Trade Representative's office. None of those options go away if Republicans lose the midterms.

"We're not going to get relief from Congress changing in the short term," said Flavio Volpe, a member of the Canada-U.S. economic advisory committee and president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association.
But if Democrats are successful, Volpe says that will mean "more adults in the room."
More threatened tariffs on horizon
With no end in sight to the trade tensions, more threatened tariffs are less than three months away.
Days after trade talks fell apart in August, Trump again complained about Canada "ripping off" the United States.
"On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts and Steel will be increased to 50%," he wrote on his Truth Social platform.
"WE DON'T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US!"

items: Lawsuit challenging Trump's tariffs against Canada filed in U.S. Court of International Trade

blocks.text: Clow says this new deadline will incentivize Canada to see if there's some sort of agreement to be made.

"Like a lot of threats we've seen from this administration you have to take it seriously even if it may not come to pass," he said. "And unfortunately we won't know until Jan. 1 whether this is a real threat."
LeBlanc noted on Power & Politics that the administration has yet to move forward with anything official on increasing auto tariffs.

"But there's no doubt that that is obviously of concern to us. That's why we continue to say to our American counterparts … that all of this is avoidable if the two countries can come to an agreement," the minister said.
When asked about the status of these possible tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer declined to provide specific details.

items: Stelco's U.S. owner says steelmaker had 'strongest' quarter since acquisition as massive layoffs underway

blocks.text: At the G20 trade ministers' summit in Milwaukee three weeks ago, Greer rejected the assertion that this is a threat and denied that Canada is being targeted.
He said tariffs are part of U.S. "domestic economic policy" and that they're "not focused on any one country."
‘Door is always open’ for U.S.-Canada trade talks, says Greer
If work is happening behind the scenes to move ahead with these new tariffs, Canadian industry officials say they have not been given any sort of heads up.
"We haven't seen any paperwork," says Volpe.

In order for a tariff threat to become a reality, it requires some form of legal documentation to bring the policy into force. Those documents outline the scope of the policy and the laws being used to enforce the levies.
"They know that if they tariff auto parts from Canada, they shut down the entire American automotive manufacturing structure simply because those parts will not get delivered," Volpe said.
While Volpe is confident the Trump administration will back away from new tariffs on auto parts, he said he isn't so sure about autos and steel.
"[Trump] just might be willing to sink Detroit trying to prove some point that nobody can understand," he said.
Canada the irritant
Trump routinely uses Canada as a punching bag in his campaign rally speeches.
"At some point, we're making a deal that's gonna be amazing," Trump said during a stop in Highland Heights, Ky., on Saturday.
"But for years we've lost billions and billions of dollars, and they just felt so emboldened."

blocks.text: Trump has long been frustrated by trade deficits, including with Canada. However, he regularly exaggerates the actual number.
He was cheered when he called Trudeau a "loser" before taking aim at Prime Minister Mark Carney.
"Your current guy's good … he's a nice guy, but he's not nice when it comes to trade," he said.
"They're learning and they're suffering."

articles.title: Selena Gomez says vaping nicotine changed her voice
articles.summary: The singer and actor posted a video online Sunday responding to ongoing discourse about her voice and why it's changed over the years. "I'm not going to be able to change my voice. I vaped nicotine a…

image.caption: Selena Gomez arrives at the Rare Impact Fund Benefit on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles. The singer said Sunday that vaping has changed her voice, but that she's since quit. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

The singer and actor posted a video online Sunday responding to ongoing discourse about her voice and why it's changed over the years. "I'm not going to be able to change my voice. I vaped nicotine a lot," she said.
'It's just not worth it,' the actor and singer said on Instagram
Selena Gomez says vaping changed her voice, in a video Sunday responding discourse about her voice over the years.

"I'm not going to be able to change my voice. I vaped nicotine a lot," the U.S. singer, actor and founder of the Rare Beauty makeup line said in a video shared to her Instagram stories, which isn't online anymore.

"Nicotine is so hard to quit, and I think I just wanted to say, if you're going through it, or if you're even trying to vape, it's just not worth it," Gomez, 34, continued. "It's so stupid, and it's changed my voice.
She laughed, while adding: "So if you guys don't like listening to my voice, that's totally understandable. I don't mind. Just don't listen to it."

items: Selena Gomez reveals lupus diagnosis, chemotherapy treatment
Selena Gomez undergoes kidney transplant due to lupus

blocks.text: Gomez didn't specify when and for how long she'd been vaping. "I stopped, and I just hope we can keep it up. It's really hard," she said.
"But I know if you are going through something, you can get through it, too."
Years of health battles
Gomez has been open about her health battles over the years.
In 2015 she shared that she was diagnosed with Lupus, a chronic autoimmune disease that occurs when an individual's immune system attacks its own healthy tissues and organs.
She has previously suggested that she thinks it had affected her vocal chords.
"Sometimes things happen. I get weird. My throat kind of swells inside sometimes. That's all."⁠ she shared in an Instagram live Q&A last year.
Gomez also received a kidney transplant in 2017 and spoke out about her bipolar disorder diagnosis in her 2022 documentary Selena Gomez: My Mind & Me.

items: Cigarette packages are getting updated labels to deter smoking, but advocates say vaping needs action, too

blocks.text: Our airways are supposed to be for breathing: expert
While Gomez is sounding the alarm, health experts point out that the dangers of vaping go far beyond nicotine.
"Our airways are supposed to be for breathing, not to have all these external things put in it," said Dilini Vethanayagam, professor of medicine at the University of Alberta.

Vethanayagam told CBC News there aren't currently any formal, large-scale clinical trials specifically focused on vaping's direct impact on the vocal cords. But the myriad chemicals in vape smoke, including but not limited to nicotine, "can affect different parts of our upper and lower airways, vocal cord included," she said.

Health Canada says there are over 1,500 unique chemicals found in vaping products and liquids. The long-term health impacts of vaping are still being studied, but health risks have been identified including lung damage, Vethanayagam noted.
Will Canada restrict flavoured vaping?
Speaking out about vaping matters
Still, Vethanayagam says honesty from public figures like Gomez matters.
"It's good that she's bringing up the vaping issue with her platform because a lot of people think it's safe and it's not — specifically to nicotine and her voice," she said.

"I'm sure she's probably seeing someone, like a physician in regards to those specific issues. But yeah, bottom line — and just like we used to say, don't do it for cigarettes, don't do it for vaping."
Gomez, left, and Benny Blanco arrive at the 83rd Golden Globes on Jan. 11, 2026, at the Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP)
Vethanayagam says vaping is "a huge potential epidemic that's been building," that requires more "stringent regulations" on their sale and use.
"It's getting better, but it's slow," she said.

In Canada, the federal government announced five years ago it would restrict vaping flavours in the face of a growing number of young people using the products, but it's currently unclear when or even whether that will happen.
Representatives from N.B. Lung are in Ottawa this week to talk to MPs about legislating restrictions on younger people to legally buy tobacco products, including vapes.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca
With files from CBC's Marina Von Stackleberg and Hannah Rudderham

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Which jobs are most vulnerable to AI replacement?
articles.summary: Among the industries that will be most impacted by AI are business process outsourcing and information technology, which are among the major employers in the Philippines.

blocks.text: While the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) has presented new opportunities, its developments have raised concerns about its impact on human labor.

In a report from GMA News Feed, voice-over artist Inka Magnaye's post about how her mother lost an acting job to AI went viral. Magnaye said that while AI is an instrument, it should not be used to replace human talent.
Workers across different industries have echoed this sentiment. But which jobs are in danger of being affected by AI?
According to the Tokyo-based think tank Asian Development Bank Institute (ADBI), 76% of work in the Philippines will be highly vulnerable to automation by the year 2030—the highest in Southeast Asia.
Among the industries that will be most impacted are business process outsourcing and information technology, which are among the major employers in the Philippines.

The Information Technology and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP) said that the industry is also expecting lower revenue. In its six-year roadmap in 2022, the industry was targeted to generate $59 billion in revenues. However, as of July 2026, this has been lowered to $43 billion to $50 billion.

The IBPAP was also expecting 2.5 million workers to be employed in the industry by 2028. But a review of the roadmap led to the projection being lowered to 1.85 million to 2.14 million. These workers, however, have switched to different employment.

"It has affected some jobs, but based on all the members we’ve talked to, the entry-level jobs that some of the AI trials have affected, those employees have been able to be redeployed,” IBPAP president Jack Madrid said.

The International Labour Organization (ILO) said that around 12.7 million workers in the Philippines have been exposed to generative AI—a type of AI that could make its own text, image, audio, video and computer code.
This does not mean that AI will replace workers immediately; tasks will just become automated.
However, 3.6% of jobs with the highest use of generative AI have a higher chance of job displacement.

According to the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers, the revenue of the music industry could be reduced by 24%, with audiovisual creators also seeing a reduction of 21% in revenue.
AI ethicist Carl Joe Javier said that this could have a greater effect on Filipino creatives.

“If we have arts, which historically have been undervalued, and then you have tech movements, which also push to undervalue art, because they're like, “I don't need artists anymore because this thing can generate images for me.” Because the tech people, they actually don't really care about art. That's not their concern. They don't care about cultural preservation,” Javier said.

Javier said that a number of companies use AI to cut costs. However, is saving money worth risking the quality of the output that a human can do? Would it be possible to put together what a human and AI could do to improve the output?

“When everyone had a computer, look at the productivity, the productivity gains. When you go to the office, and everyone has a computer. Because in the old days, not everyone was assigned a computer. Now that we all have smartphones, we are more productive than we ever were. But none of those devices involved the removal of people,” he said.

Many experts still believe that AI could not replace humans in the workplace. The Harvard Business School said that AI does not have emotional intelligence to solve interpersonal conflict or understand human behavior.
Only humans could make a human connection. AI could still help lighten the load, however.
The ILO had suggested targeting regional and sectoral policies to make sure that people could benefit from generative AI. Workers should be prepared for the changes that this technology could bring.
Workers vulnerable to AI replacement should also be protected.

“I do think that everyone should be pressuring their legislators to pass legislation and regulation. And hindi lang parang may budget for upskilling…All these technologies continue to change the world; how are we going to imagine and situate ourselves within this world? And how are we going to imagine our workforce and our economy within that context? So, kailangan, sana, we have people who are pushing in that direction,” Javier said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations
articles.summary: Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m

blocks.text: A senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backers Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo would be legal under the proposed new foreign donors cap three months before they gave £72m to the party.

James Orr, who was then Reform UK’s head of policy and a Cambridge professor, discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim.

A reporter was posing as a potential donor when Orr talked to him about “filling the war chest in anticipation” of tougher donations rules, describing it as the establishment trying to “kneecap” the party.

Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after Channel 4 broadcast some of Verbatim’s undercover filming in which he appeared to discuss ways to get around funding laws to allow donations from a US-based donor.
The matter is under police investigation and he remains suspended, although Reform has released its own report clearing Orr and another official of wrongdoing.

The new footage has been shared with the Guardian after a public debate about whether the two £36m donations from Harborne and Delo to Reform UK will be allowed under the cap. The party maintains the donations are legal, pointing out that the retrospective overseas donor cap has not yet been passed into law.

In the footage, recorded in July this year, Orr expressed doubt about whether Delo and Harborne would still be able to donate given, when it does become law, the £100,000 overseas donor cap is to cover party donations dating back to March this year.

Orr believed Delo would probably meet the residency test as long as he was not required to have been a tax resident, in which case he would be “stuffed”. He said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge” in terms of avoiding the overseas cap and he “can’t do anything for 12 months” after moving back.
Harborne had been living in Thailand until he registered to vote in Hampshire this summer, and Delo has long been resident in Hong Kong, though he has been on the UK domestic register for some years.

The new law will put a £100,000 limit on how much overseas donors can give to a political party. It will apply to donations made after March 2026, and will require any domestic donor who wants to give more than £100,000 to have been resident in the UK for at least a calendar year.

In the discussion, Orr was recorded as saying the party was too reliant on Harborne and Delo as “two big whales”. He said the new law was “a retrospective law, which is unheard of. So, we’re going to challenge it in the courts.”

Orr added: “We’ll push it through judicial review. And then … so, we’ll have a big fight. But, yeah, the last few days we’ve been working hard on just filling the war chest as best we can, in anticipation of something quite brutal.”

On whether the two men would be caught by the overseas cap, he said: “I mean, there’s going to be a huge fight over that. But Ben, I think it’s probably OK, because I think he is … it depends on how they legislate it, they might just say, you must have been tax domiciled here for X period of time, in which case Ben is stuffed.”

Orr went on to say: “It depends what … test for moving back you apply. So, under the common law, there’s a two-limb test, which is actually quite a – not a stringent one. It’s a factual thing, a factual matrix test.

“How much time you spend in England, do you have a house here, can you vote, do you have any bills that you pay, you know, it’s quite kind of, it’s not tax … So, on that test, Ben meets it, I think. And then the second then is intention. Do you intend to stay, so, evidence that you intend to stay …”
after newsletter promotion

Having debated whether Delo would meet the test, Orr said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge”. The Reform official said he would move back to the UK. “But, if he does move back, there’s 12 – he can’t pay – he can’t do anything for 12 months. And, it looks as if they will bring that in.”

In his chat with the undercover reporter, Orr also referred to the “complicated backstory” of Delo, a British-born billionaire who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business. He was later pardoned by Donald Trump.
Orr also spoke about having spent time on Delo’s yacht in the Peloponnese this summer, talking of mixing work and a holiday in Greece, saying: “We went from Athens down to Ben’s boat in Porto Cheli.”
A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back.”

Orr did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to electoral laws on overseas funding and dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.

Lawyers for Harborne described Orr’s comments as private speculation which it would not be appropriate to comment on and did not represent established facts. Delo’s lawyers did not respond substantively, saying he would not be drawn into speculation about a conversation he was not party to, or the legal effect of a law yet to be passed.
Reform has previously said it intends to take legal action against Verbatim and its directors over the undercover filming.

articles.title: Jackdaw North Sea gasfield to get go-ahead in blow to climate campaigners
articles.summary:
Move signals Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea industry but threatens to undermine Labour’s green credentials

The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, in a move…

blocks.text: The Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, in a move that signals Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry but threatens to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs.

Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, , the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments.

The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it.
But it will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.

Tessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”
She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”

blocks.caption: Activists from Fossil Free London stage a protest against the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.  Photograph: Vuk Valcic/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: When fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production.

Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status had become totemic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated.
The field was approved by the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting they would have to make a decision on either Jackdaw or Rosebank.
However both fields were cast into doubt last year by a landmark ruling that said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted.

A judge ruled that regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas that the two fields will produce when deciding whether they would violate the UK’s climate commitments.

Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it.

Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from the US president, Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”.
Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the president’s arguments earlier this summer, promising to take a “pragmatic approach” to the decision.
“There is a resource there,” he added in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.”
He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas, we will set out our decisions shortly.”

Multiple sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has now decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns.

She will make the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, on Wednesday. They will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence.

Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later in the year.
The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in the north-east of Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.
But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.

A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.
That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18-24-year-olds.
Ellie Mae O’Hagan, UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.

“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”

Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it will produce around seven times the CO2 emissions and partly because most of the oil produced there will be exported.

Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”

articles.title: Russell Brand told woman to ‘clear up the mess you’ve made’ after alleged rape, court hears
articles.summary:
Woman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home after gig was one of most painful experiences of her life

A woman has said she “couldn’t speak or breathe” when Russell Brand raped her…

blocks.text: A woman has said she “couldn’t speak or breathe” when Russell Brand raped her at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd after one of his gigs, a court has heard.
She said the comedian looked “horrified” after the alleged attack so she assumed he would apologise but instead he told her: “Clear up the mess you’ve made.”
The woman said she “tortured herself” in the years that followed because it was one of the “most painful experiences” of her life.

Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.
The TV personality sat upright in the dock as the woman’s video-recorded police interview was played to Southwark crown court on Tuesday.
The woman told officers she was a “massive fan” of Brand and “giddy” to meet him after one of his stand-up performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.
She alleged he pointed to her and said “you” before inviting her, her friend and a third young woman they did not know to have drinks with him.

Brand’s security guard later invited the trio backstage where the woman performed oral sex on the actor but refused to have penetrative sex. By then, the woman’s friend had left, but Brand had sex on a sofa with the third woman, who was 19.

The woman said she felt “awful” and “disgusting” when she left the dressing room, which is when Brand asked her why she had refused to have sex with him. She told him she had a boyfriend, to which he replied: “We don’t belong to anyone, we’re all free, the ownership of people is sort of what we’ve been sold.”

blocks.caption: The woman said Brand was ‘persuasive’ about her visiting his three-storey townhouse in Hampstead, west London. Photograph: Wenn Rights Ltd/Alamy

blocks.text: Brand asked for her phone number and began messaging and calling her. She said he was “persuasive” about her visiting his three-storey townhouse in Hampstead, north-west London.

Days later, the woman was picked up by Brand’s driver and taken to the star’s home knowing she would have sex with him. “I’ve really struggled for a really long time to accept what happened to me, because I went there knowingly and willingly,” she said.

She alleged that when she arrived, Brand told her: “This is the best decision you’ve made.” But when they went to Brand’s bedroom, he ordered her to have a shower because her hair smelled “funny”, and made her brush her teeth.

She said it made her feel “really dirty”, adding: “At the time it did feel like a thrilling thing to go to the house of this person I really fancied, and I loved comedy. But all those things didn’t feel that good.”

blocks.caption: The woman described Brand’s dark bedroom and ‘enormous’ bed.  Photograph: Metropolitan Police

blocks.text: She described his dark bedroom and “enormous” bed, and the distinctive black toilet paper in his ensuite bathroom. Pictures later shown to the jury showed a crucifix above his bed and black furnishings.
The woman told how they had consensual vaginal sex but that she did not enjoy the experience, saying: “It felt very awkward. It didn’t matter who I was, and I just sort of wanted it to be over.”

Then Brand anally raped the woman, she told police. “He didn’t give me a warning, he didn’t ask,” she said. “I don’t know how long it took for me between it going on and me asking him to stop. I don’t think it was very long. I felt like I couldn’t speak or breathe, the amount of pain.”
She alleged she begged him to stop, at first really quietly and then more loudly, but Brand continued.
She said he looked “absolutely fucking horrified” after the alleged attack, adding: “I thought he was going to say sorry … but actually what he said was: ‘You need to clear up the mess you’ve made.’”
She said one of Brand’s aides later asked her to leave because the comedian had a gig.
“The way I would describe that event to people after was that it was traumatic and that he hurt me and harmed me. And when I asked him to stop, he didn’t,” she said.
She told the court she had gone to a sexual health clinic afterwards because she feared she had HIV, and she became unwell and anxious.

“In the years that followed, if I spoke to people about it, it was was very much laced with ‘I shouldn’t have gone’, and I think I tortured myself because I think it was one of the most painful experiences I’d gone through.”
Earlier on Tuesday, two women who have separately accused Brand of sexually assaulting them at work in front of his entourage gave evidence from behind a screen.
The first woman said Brand laughed after “mauling” her by squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at a radio station in 2004 or 2005.
She told the court he “overpowered her with such strength” during the “violent” and “frenzied” attack that took place in the middle of her work day.
She said she had “buried” the assault because there was such a culture of fear in the media in the 2000s and Brand was a “big star”.
The second woman, who worked at Channel 4, said she was “repulsed” when Brand placed his head in her lap during a filming project after she was asked to give him a massage.
She said Brand was with two men – named in court as Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy – during the alleged assault in 2009, which she reported to her line manager.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Lebanon faces uncertainty as UNIFIL mandate nears end
articles.summary: As UN peacekeeping forces prepare to withdraw from Lebanon, Israel remains present and Hezbollah is still armed. A new EU support mission aims to strengthen Lebanon's army, but will not replace UN…

image.caption: Thousands of troops are due to leave Lebanon as the UNIFIL mandate ends on December 31, 2026, prompting fears of a security vacuum Image: Mahmoud Zayyat/AFP

blocks.text: As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL, nears its end, uncertainty over the future of southern Lebanon is growing. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has warned of the need to "avert the vacuum that UNIFIL's withdrawal could create, were it to take place without agreement on a new international force to replace it."

The Lebanese government has also been pushing for a last-minute extension of UNIFIL's mandate, but so far without success. It is most likely that the 7,565 peacekeepers from 46 countries will begin withdrawing from the UN-patrolled so-called Blue Line zone on December 31, 2026.

The Blue Line, which stretches for 120 kilometers (75 miles), is a UN-identified line of withdrawal between Israel and Lebanon, not an internationally agreed border. It was established in 2000. However, as early as in 1978, multinational UNIFIL troops were deployed to this region to monitor the area after Israel invaded Lebanon in response to attacks by Palestinian armed groups.

After the 2006 Israel-Hezbollah war, the mandate was expanded to support the Lebanese army in implementing UN Security Council Resolution 1701. The resolution calls for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River to be free of armed personnel, assets and weapons other than those belonging to the Lebanese government and UNIFIL. It also calls for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.

However, following cross-border attacks by Hezbollah in October 2023 and the ensuing war in 2024, Israel has been occupying large swaths of Lebanese territory in a self-declared security zone called the Yellow Line, which is located north of the Blue Line.

Of the more than 1.2 million people displaced in Lebanon during the renewed conflict in 2026, around 329,000 remained internally displaced as of September 29, according to the International Organization for Migration. Israel has also caused extensive destruction to homes and key infrastructure in southern Lebanon, saying it needs to protect its citizens in northern Israel from attacks launched from the area.

Hezbollah — which is designated as a terrorist organization by several countries, including the United States and Germany, while the European Union designates its armed wing as a terrorist organization — continues to reject disarmament, citing the need to defend itself for as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Hezbollah is also closely linked to Iran, and in case of renewed conflict between Iran and Israel, it's likely that Hezbollah would open a second front in Israel's north in support of Iran.

blocks.caption: Around 1.2 million people were displaced in Lebanon this year. However, the majority have since returned to their homes in the southImage: Mohammed Zaatari/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The situation in southern Lebanon remains tense," Kandice Ardiel, UNIFIL's spokesperson, told DW. "We are seeing continued Israeli military operations, including overflights of Lebanese airspace by jets, helicopters and drones, airstrikes, artillery strikes and mortar fire."

"Until our mandate ends on December 31, we continue to monitor and report what is happening, and we are liaising between the parties on a daily basis to ensure safe movements of civilians, humanitarian aid, and peacekeeping patrols," she said, adding that the drawdown and withdrawal would then take place in stages.

The end of the mandate also means the end of the mission for thousands of UNIFIL troops in southern Lebanon. "People have built careers, friendships, skills and a sense of purpose together," Ardiel said. "Endings are never easy, especially when there is a sense that the work we do is still needed."
Beirut's lack of authority, money compounds disarmament dilemma
The upcoming withdrawal of UNIFIL also highlights two major dilemmas for Lebanon's government.

"Beirut is concerned that violations of any agreements, whether on the Israeli or the Hezbollah side, can't be tracked in the absence of an international military force," Paul Shaya, a Washington-based Middle East researcher and adjunct professor at George Washington University, told DW.

Furthermore, after years of political deadlock, the COVID-19 pandemic, soaring inflation and economic crises, the Beirut port blast in 2020 and the destruction caused by the 2024 war between Israel and Hezbollah, Lebanon's economic lifeline depends on international funding. However, a large share of the much-needed investment from the United States and Gulf states is tied to Hezbollah's disarmament.
"Ultimately, it is going to be dependent on President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam to secure sufficient funding and resources to support the Lebanese military," said Shaya.
Can Lebanon's peace experiment work?

Until that happens, Aoun and Salam have very limited options for disarming Hezbollah, said David Wood, Lebanon researcher at the International Crisis Group. "They have opened direct talks with Israel to bring about an end to the disastrous conflict, but that process includes neither Hezbollah nor its backer Iran — both of which oppose the group's disarmament," he said.

In Wood's view, Beirut has few bargaining chips in negotiations with Israel because it has been unable to secure Hezbollah's compliance. He is also worried that Lebanon's leaders have little leverage to force Hezbollah to surrender its weapons, as this could trigger a deadly domestic conflict in the country. In the past, Hezbollah has openly warned that trying to seize its weapons by force would lead to war.

Despite Israel's destruction of many Hezbollah tunnels and weapons-storage facilities in Hezbollah-dominated areas in southern Lebanon and parts of Beirut, the limitation or disruption of supply routes due to the wider Iran war, as well as the fall of their ally, Syrian President Bashar Assad, observers say Hezbollah remains better equipped than the Lebanese armed forces.
Could the new EU mission replace UNIFIL in Lebanon?
On October 12, European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, with an initial three-year mandate.
"It has a civilian and military pillar," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, adding that "this is highly welcomed by the local authorities."

blocks.caption: The Iran-backed Hezbollah group maintains a political arm as well as a military arm in LebanonImage: Hussein Malla/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the European Council, the mission is to contribute to peace and security in Lebanon by strengthening the capabilities of the Lebanese armed forces and internal security forces, including in border security in accordance with the UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
However, the mission is not intended to replace UNIFIL. Rather than deploying peacekeepers to patrol southern Lebanon, it is set to initially operate north of the Litani River.

Several existing UNIFIL contributors, including Italy, France, Spain, Ireland, Germany, Austria, Finland and Poland, already expressed interest in contributing personnel and resources to the new EUSM Lebanon mission.

For the government in Beirut, this is a positive signal, noted Shaya. He added that Lebanese society also strongly supports the Lebanese military, "which many see as the only institution in the country that can uphold Lebanon's sovereignty and represent the entire country."

articles.title: Sudan drone strike kills around 150 in Abyei market
articles.summary: A drone strike hit a market in the Abyei border region disputed by Sudan and South Sudan and killed dozens. The drone caused a large fire when it hit a fuel depot. South Sudanese officials blamed…

image.caption: Medical workers, including from Medecins Sans Frontieres, worked to treat the wounded at the nearby Ameth Bek hospitalImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: A drone strike in a busy market in the disputed region of Abyei has killed more than 150 people, according to local officials.

South Sudanese officials blamed Sudan's military for the attack, without providing evidence, amid the long-running civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which is reportedly active in the Abyei area.

The special UN mission in Abyei warned in May that the RSF's presence in the resource-rich region had put residents in additional danger, and risked intensifying the older territorial dispute between Sudan and the world's newest sovereign state, South Sudan.

blocks.caption: Satellite images gave a sense of the scale of the damage after the large fire triggered by the drone strikesImage: Planet Labs PBC/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the drone strike?
According to local authorities, the attack hit the busy Amiet Market at around midday on Monday.

Yohana Akol Ngor, the caretaker information minister in Abyei, told Reuters news agency on Tuesday that the death toll had more than doubled, reaching at least 153 compared to a stated figure of 73 the previous day.
He said that Sudan's military was responsible for the attack but did not provide evidence. Akol Ngor said around 8,000 people had been displaced by the bombing.
South Sudan's Foreign Ministry also blamed the Sudanese army and said the drone struck multiple locations around the busy market.
One of these, judging by witness accounts, was a fuel depot — and this led to a large fire that proved difficult to bring under control overnight and was still ablaze on Tuesday.
South Sudan said it had summoned Sudan's ambassador to protest and urged Sudan to "refrain from any actions that endanger civilian lives and property."
Medical charity Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders, said that its staff was treating some 20 wounded people at the nearby Ameth Bek hospital.
"So far we received over 20 patients, including several critical cases. Patients with burns were also admitted," said Dr. Christian Lindauer, MSF's medical activities manager at the hospital.

blocks.caption: Many of the wounded were taken to Ameth Bek hospital for treatmentImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: What's the backstory of Sudan, South Sudan and Abyei?
The oil-rich Abyei region's status was not resolved by the 2005 peace agreement that broadly ended decades of civil war in Sudan.
It was also not settled in 2011 when South Sudan became an independent country.

A referendum was planned but never materialized, stalling over disputes on who should be allowed to vote. This left Abyei in a state of limbo, jointly administered and with an interim UN security force on site for 15 years.
The region's majority Ngok Dinka population favors joining South Sudan, while Misseriya nomads who use its pastures favor Sudan.
Amiet Market, the site of the attack, is an important trading hub for both communities.
The unstable region has also experienced intercommunal violence in recent years between Ngok Dinka and neighboring Twic Dinka communities and is home to other armed militias.

blocks.caption: Medecins Sans Frontieres said its staff were providing surgical services, wound dressing and other emergency care to more than 20 woundedImage: Medecins Sans Frontieres/REUTERS

blocks.text: How does this fit into Sudan's army's war with the RSF?

The April 2023 outbreak of fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary — which has turned into a conflict with fairly entrenched battle lines, putting Sudan into a de facto state of partition — is increasing tension in the already-strained region.
Abyei borders South Kordofan state in Sudan, which has become a major center of fighting in the war.
Sudan's military alleges that the RSF is also operating out of Abyei. The United Nations Interim Security Force for Abyei (UNISFA) issued a similar statement in May.
Officials in Abyei and South Sudan dispute this, however.
Sudan's military and the RSF have both been using drones extensively in the conflict.

"We remain alarmed by the relentless drone attacks across Sudan, as well as the damage they are causing to critical infrastructure — these attacks are taking a devastating toll on communities already struggling with the consequences of more than three years of conflict," UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters in New York on Tuesday when asked about the attack.
Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid
